facts.statement: Suskityrannus is a small tyrannosauroid theropod whose name means "coyote tyrant".
facts.quote: Suskityrannus (meaning "coyote tyrant", suski meaning "coyote" in Zuni) is a genus of small tyrannosauroid theropod from the Late Cretaceous of southern Laramidia.

facts.statement: The original fossils were discovered in 1998 by geologist Robert Denton and teenager Sterling Nesbitt during an excavation led by Doug Wolfe.
facts.quote: The original fossils were found in 1998 by Robert Denton, a professional geologist from Virginia, and a native Mesa teen Sterling Nesbitt, who was a museum volunteer that came to a dig with paleontologist Doug Wolfe.

facts.statement: The holotype and paratype specimens are preserved in the collections of the Arizona Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: Both the holotype specimen MSM P4754 (partially articulated skull and a few postcranial bones) and the paratype specimen MSM P6178 (partially articulated and associated remains including a few skull bones and an incomplete postcranial skeleton) are preserved in the collections of the Arizona Museum of Natural History

facts.statement: Known specimens of Suskityrannus have skulls measuring between 25 and 32 cm in length.
facts.quote: Suskityrannus is a small tyrannosaur, with the skull of known specimens measuring 25 - 32 cm long

facts.statement: The known specimens of Suskityrannus were approximately one meter tall, three meters long, and weighed between 20 and 40 kilograms.
facts.quote: Los dos especímenes de Suskityrannus medían aproximadamente un metro de altura y alrededor de tres metros de longitud, pesando entre 20 a 40 kilogramos.

facts.statement: Bone ring analysis concluded that one of the specimens was approximately 3 years old.
facts.quote: Se concluyó que uno de los ejemplares tendría una edad de 3 años con base en análisis de sus anillos óseos.

facts.statement: The skull and feet of Suskityrannus are much thinner than those of other tyrannosauroids.
facts.quote: Tanto el cráneo como los pies de Suskityrannus son mucho más delgados que los de otros tiranosauroideos.

facts.statement: Suskityrannus possessed key tyrannosauroid body plan traits, including the oldest known phylogenetic record of an arctometatarsalian foot in tyrannosauroids.
facts.quote: Esta especie ya poseía muchos de los rasgos clave del plan corporal de los tiranosauroideos, incluyendo el más antiguo registro filogenético del pie con arctometatarso en los tiranosauroideos.

facts.statement: The type specimen was found in the Turonian-aged Moreno Hill Formation of the Zuni Basin in western New Mexico.
facts.quote: the type specimen was found in the Turonian-aged Moreno Hill Formation of the Zuni Basin in western New Mexico.

facts.statement: Suskityrannus hazelae lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 92 million years ago, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: Suskityrannus hazelae es la única especie conocida del género extinto Suskityrannus de dinosaurio terópodo tiranosauroideo que vivió a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 92 millones de años, durante el Turoniense, en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Suskityrannus lived between 93.9 and 89.8 million years ago during the Turonian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Turonian to Turonian (93.9 to 89.8 million years ago)

facts.statement: As one of the most basal tyrannosauroid forms, Suskityrannus had a U-shaped snout and an arctometatarsalian foot.
facts.quote: Por ejemplo, como una de las formas de tiranosauroide más básicas, el animal tiene un hocico en forma de U y un pie arctometatarsiano.

facts.statement: Suskityrannus shows early adaptations to a combination of greater bite force and a more active running lifestyle.
facts.quote: Por lo tanto, muestra adaptaciones tempranas a una combinación de mayor fuerza de mordida y un estilo de vida de carrera más activo.

facts.statement: The original 1998 identification of Suskityrannus as a dromaeosaurid was not based on an exhaustive examination of the animal.
facts.quote: La determinación original como dromeosáurido en 1998 no se basó en un examen exhaustivo del animal.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the initial misidentification as a dromaeosaurid was influenced by the popularity of Jurassic Park and the lack of conflict with the fossil's size, location, and age.
facts.quote: En la década de 1990, los dromeosáuridos eran muy populares como resultado de Jurassic Park , y dado que el tamaño, la ubicación y la edad geológica no entraban en conflicto con tal identificación, era natural verlos como un pariente de Velociraptor.

facts.statement: In 2019, Suskityrannus was placed basally in Tyrannosauroidea, just below Timurlengia in the family tree, making it one of the few known mid-Cretaceous tyrannosauroids.
facts.quote: En 2019, Suskityrannus se colocó basalmente en Tyrannosauroidea, justo debajo de Timurlengia en el árbol genealógico, uno de los pocos tiranosauroides conocidos de mediados del período Cretácico.

rejected.statement: Suskityrannus was formally described as a genus of primitive tyrannosauroid in 2019.
rejected.quote: In 2019 Suskityrannus was formally described as a genus of primitive tyrannosauroid.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'was formally described as a genus of primitive'

rejected.statement: Histological analysis suggests that adult Suskityrannus would have been significantly smaller than mature tyrannosaurids from later periods.
rejected.quote: The holotype and the paratype belong to young individuals that didn't reach skeletal maturity, but the histological analyses revealed that the bone tissues and vascularization are different from those found in young individuals of large-bodied tyrannosaurids during the Campanian-Maastrichtian age, so the adults would have been significantly smaller than mature tyrannosaurids.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'would have been significantly smaller than mature tyrannosaurids'

rejected.statement: Prior to its formal description, Suskityrannus was informally referred to as the "Zuni coelurosaur", "Zuni tyrannosaur", and "Zunityrannus" in the 2011 documentary Planet Dinosaur.
